[h2]Context of the Review[/h2]
As someone who came into KCDII without playing the first game, I did not have any expectations beyond the media and user reviews. I also purchased it about 9 months after release, so I played a version built upon months of patches and DLC releases. Additionally, I played and finished the storyline of KCDII almost one year ago, so my memory is fuzzy. However, I stand by my opinion that KCDII is a fantastic game that I highly recommend to any fan of open-world RPGs. 

[h2]Narrative and Characters[/h2]
The narrative of KCDII delivers in spades. I possess no applicable knowledge of 15th-century European history, so much of the first act had an air of mystery as I navigated interpersonal relationships and alliances. 

The characters presented to you are ALIVE! From Hans Capon and your immediate circle to the smallest of side characters, the world is rich with characters of depth. Even the characters you grow to despise are only able to elicit this reaction because of how well they are written and performed. Despite the time since I played, I can still remember three specific characters off the top of my head who had me imagining how Henry was going to deliver their comeuppance. To emphasize the depth of story, two of these are side-plot characters! 

I would often walk away from quests feeling satisfied. Many plotlines and side characters, no matter how small, were impactful to my playing experience. 

[h2]RPG Elements[/h2]
The RPG elements of character progression may be the magnum opus of KCDII. Never in a video game have I genuinely felt so immersed in a character. In the beginning, without mentioning any plot points, you are a feeble, inept commoner without any notable skills. Alchemy is a new domain to you, social situations are a minefield, and you'd best forget about posing any kind of threat in combat. 

However, at the same pace you as a player learn and develop your skills in the gameplay mechanics of KCDII, Henry also learns and develops his own ability. While it can be boiled down on paper to "do X thing Y times to unlock Z ability," this was not my perception of the gameplay progression. Perhaps others can articulate my experience better than I can, but I truly felt rewarded for my efforts to get better at the game, and it seemed deliberately built as a shared journey between me and Henry.

[h2]Combat[/h2]
Combat is clunky, and I won't pretend otherwise. Early fights can feel awkward and punishing, and it takes time before anything clicks. But learning it is genuinely satisfying. Unlike most RPGs, where you eventually out-level your enemies until fights become trivial, KCDII made me feel like I won because I'd actually gotten better at fighting. By the late game, I felt like I had mastered the combat myself, and that sense of earned skill is something few games deliver.

[h2]The DLC Issue - A Personal Gripe with RPGs in General[/h2]
[h3]No spoilers version[/h3]
Many aging RPG titles suffer from blending DLC perks (typically equipment) and storylines into a world, story, and character/equipment progression that were designed without them. Low-level characters have OP equipment and storylines make less sense because of conflicts between the base-game narrative and expansion storylines. I wish there had been a way to toggle the introduction of certain DLCs to later points in the game, or to have them locked behind a small gate of accomplishment to better introduce them. KCDII does this to some extent, but not enough. 

Of course, a player can choose not to use the OP crossbow and armor that inexplicably found their way into my chest, but the intentional choice to [i]not[/i] use it is more immersion-breaking and distracting than if it had been introduced in a way more in line with the rest of the game.

[h3]Spoilers for mid to late game and Legacy of the Forge[/h3]
[spoiler]I cannot remember exact specifics, but I really feel like the final act of the game was worsened by the existence of the Legacy of the Forge expansion, or at least its prominence. At the same time that you are an outlaw in the land with powerful figures wanting your head, you are an established, well-known blacksmith in Kuttenberg. I mean, I quite literally killed dozens of men defending the Jewish Quarter and had been ousted from town, but then I just waltz back in the front door of the city and go about my blacksmithing trade. I also made copious amounts of money from selling my works, and even fixed the clock tower, but when I return to the main story I am an underground vagabond plotting the heist of the century. Had I known how it would influence the game by giving me a home base in town, and how it would break my immersion in the story, I would have chosen to not pursue its questline as early as I did.[/spoiler]

[h2]Verdict[/h2]
My DLC complaints are minor next to everything KCDII gets right. It has memorable, well-written characters, a story that kept me invested down to its side quests, and a progression system, combat included, that made me feel like I was growing alongside Henry. If you enjoy open-world RPGs, it's well worth your time, even if you've never touched the first game.

[h3] Story, Dialogues & Pacing [/h3]
On a personal level, I'm not a big fan of plotlines heavily focused on high-stakes kingdom politics, kings, and grand court intrigue. Because of this, I actually liked the first game slightly more: it had a grounded, "local" narrative that felt more personal. Here, the sheer scale of kingdom affairs felt a bit suffocating and tedious at times

On top of that, some dialogues drag on for way too long. Massive exposition dumps aren't really my thing, so I fast-read and skipped a lot. By the time I reached around 60–70% completion, I was skipping most of the dialogues entirely

[h3] Romance Mechanics [/h3]
The romance system felt quite unpolished, which was disappointing

[spoiler]
You don't really get to see anything meaningful regarding Theresa. I initially aimed for a secret ending with her, but as the story progressed, I realized Katherine was a fantastic romance option. Choosing Katherine over Theresa felt right for me because, while Theresa is a genuinely GOOD GIRL, I didn't feel a strong emotional connection to her in the first game, whereas I developed strong feelings for Katherine here

However, the ending with Katherine feels way too open-ended. Once the main story wraps up, you barely have any options to interact with her, and she acts as if nothing happened between you two. I understand this setup makes sense contextually, as the finale clearly tees up a sequel, but I still expected a few more interaction options post-ending

I have a deep love hate relationship with this game. I have never completed a game and felt such complex emotions. It is one of the most rewarding, realistic, and incredible games I have ever played. At the same time, it is one of the most difficult, frustrating, and overwhelming games I have ever played by far. The ability to save is few and far between and the devs make it much more difficult than it needs to be which does take away from the joy and fun of the game. I am extremely disappointed by the unnecessary amount of violence towards dogs in the game. It does not impact the story, has no point, and should not be in the story at all. It took away from the beauty of the game for me and the enjoyment I got out of it. It was not needed and I hope whoever added those moments into the story does not have animals of their own. There is clearly something very wrong with them. Overall, the story was rich and incredibly detailed. It was inspiring and breathtaking. Graphics are great and the intelligence of the NPC's is scary good. They are highly intelligent and observant. Some of the best NPC's I have ever seen. Very similar to RDR2 in that way. I loved Mutt and what he brought to the experience, it would not have been as good as it was without him. Not even close. It was so cool to have a partner in crime. I loved the depth of the lore and the tedious process of building your character. My favorite part of the game was stealth and stealing. Every chance I got, I would have fun with sneaking around, stealing stuff, and seeing how much money I could get for it. I really enjoyed outsmarting the NPC‘s and seeing how much I could get away with. I absolutely loved the challenge of figuring out people’s schedules and how to get in and out of houses or businesses and how to navigate that entire process. It never got boring for me. The game is extremely detailed, very difficult, and at times mind numbingly frustrating. I have never been so frustrated playing a game in my entire life. You truly have to grind and survive in every sense. Nothing will come easy. You will die more times than you ever have in any game you have ever played. You will feel like an idiot. Constantly. It will test your patience and you will have to google A LOT to figure out what is going on, where you are supposed to go, and what you are supposed to do. The devs do not explain much and I think that is another unfortunate issue with this game. If i did not look up all that I did, I would have missed a tremendous amount of story telling and I truly do not think I would have completed the game. It was that hard. I have never not completed a game. I have been gaming for 25 years. Every genre you can think of, I have played it. This game almost broke me. There are so many mission that leave you very stuck, confused, overwhelmed, and frustrated with little to no guidance. Combat is a nightmare. It is the hardest combat I have ever encountered. I never really got better lol. I just some how got by (or lucky). I think there is a fine line between overwhelming the player to the point that they do not want to go back to the game and creating a challenging game that is enjoyable. Not going to lie, when the main story was over, I was relieved. Sad that the story ended, but glad that the grind was over. I don't like feeling that way at the end of a game. I want to be left wanting more. I hope this is something they work on in the future for KCD3. The entire game should not be an extreme grind. The point of playing a game is to escape and have FUN. I hope the devs keep that in mind and listen to the many players that feel the same way I do. I love this game and I hate this game. I am glad I played it because it did help me through a difficult time in my life. I put nearly 200 hours into this game and I still have a few more quests to do after finishing the main story. This game will always have a special place in my heart and I am glad I played it. The characters are wonderful and the story telling was epic. It truly pulls you in and takes hold of you. There is nothing quite like it.

Kingdom Come: Deliverance II is a direct sequel to the original game, taking place shortly after the events of the first game. You once again play as Henry of Skalitz, and you are sent by your lord as an envoy/diplomat to deliver a very important letter to a neighboring town. However, things don't go according to plan, and sh*t hits the fan really quickly.

[b] Story: [/b]
The story is really compelling from start to finish and takes place across two different regions: Trosky, which serves as the beginner zone, and later, Kuttenberg. I was surprised by the massive scale of the game and its attention to detail. The game also features a lot of choices that affect how things play out, and I think there are around three different endings, depending on what you do throughout the game.
When it comes to romance, there are also a lot of different characters you can court and romance. I recommend getting the Legacy of the Forge DLC, which features a hilarious and insanely long questline. The 10-minute ending cutscene almost made me die of laughter before nearly bringing me to tears at the end.

[b] Characters: [/b]
I honestly can't think of a single bad character in this game. Every character you meet feels fleshed out and interesting in their own way. The main characters are really intriguing, and the quests are a lot of fun. You also get to meet (and, at times, play as) Godwin, the priest from the first game, which is great since he was one of my favorite characters. The overall dialogue is fun and engaging, but can feel a bit stiff sometimes.

[b] Combat: [/b]
The only real downside to this game is the combat. It's a bit better than in the first game, but the lock-on fighting system made me rage so many times. Every strike can be lethal, and timing, blocking, and riposting are crucial to making it out alive. If you miss once, it could be game over.
I eventually just ended up poisoning my blade to take down my enemies one by one. Otherwise, I'd resort to using a longbow or crossbow with poisoned ammunition.

[b] Overall: [/b]
Kingdom Come: Deliverance II is hands down one of the best medieval action RPGs out there. The attention to detail is beyond anything I've ever seen in a game.
I waited a year before playing it, so my experience was pretty much bug-free (apart from a few crashes during loading), and the game ran smoothly throughout my playthrough. The atmosphere, historical accuracy and overall setting and vibe of medieval Bohemia are insanely good, and the best I've ever seen.

I highly recommend it if you're a fan of games like The Elder Scrolls (e.g., Oblivion and Skyrim), but be prepared to get a bit aggravated by the melee combat and fighting system. Then again, the game has access to the Steam workshop, so you can mod it how you like it.

This is my love letter to Kingdom Come Deliverance 2.

This game is a masterpiece, my absolute most favourite video game ever made! Of course this is a personal opinion, MY OPINION and how I FEEL about this game. That said, I started a new game in hardcore mode which should be a worse experience because of the debuffs. But man It just makes the game more realistic and it slows down the game so much! Which sounds like a bad thing, IF you don't love every little detail. This way you need to walk around the wilderness, witness details you never noticed before. Slow down and take in the games towns, villages, NPCs and small details. It is a totally different, better experience to the base game. Well of course, for certain people, I admit it's not for everyone.

So let's get into the review. Gameplay wise the game is a huge improvement form the first one. The first game was an Indie game made by a small passionate studio. The second the in fact was made by the same little passionate studio BUT with the budget of a TRIPLE A game. That means it's just so fluid and every little mechanic feels just right.  I did not feel anything would be forced, everything fell in place. Dialogs and choices are made so well, you can solve encounters with so many options, stealth, strenght, wit or speech. You're choice, the game let's you decide, it is just a bloody awesome RPG what more do you want? It does not feel like you are the main character you are a nobody in a medieval setting. Grunt fantasy in medieval bohemia?! Sounds lovely doesn't it? Of course it is. You do not feel overpowered, more underpowered to be honest. Especially if fighting outnumbered without gear. You WILL die. But after struggling through and learning and getting armour. You will be able to fight outnumbered and it will feel so satisfying. The game is a struggle especially for beginners but that makes it more fun, you will enjoy the boring bits, brewing potions and crafting, walking from places discovering the map. This is what makes KCD2 feel so different. It makes you slow down and enjoy boring tasks. Sounds weird but you need to experience it to understand. 

Combat is a little dumbed down from KCD 1, but it feels better, easier in way because of the decrease of attack angles, combo wise I feel it's about the same. The sword is absolutely broken compared to other weapons. Better said masterstrike is broken, you can easily beat the game by just using masterstrike. Polearms are a cool such as crosbows and guns. Battles feel better and yes bigger as well, sieges are absolutely cool. There are people who prefered the harder KCD1 combat but this is a mainstream game meant for wide audiences, combat was change for this reason. If you want harder I am sure there are mods for that.

Graphics are godlike I played on one below the max settings. Everything is just so pretty, this is probably the biggest change from the first game. Trosky region is a nature powerhouse, you just want to take a forest walk after a forest walk and go down to the ponds, follow the rivers climb up the mountains go trough the valleys and so on. It just feels real. Like you are in medieval Bohemia admiring the beauty of the region. 

Sounds, I played it in Czech but I know the English dubbing is awesome as well. The actors just nailed everything, hungarian needs some improvements in some aspects. Music, Jan Valta made an absolute banger soundtrack. Capturing the vibe of medieval Bohemia. Ambiences of regions of places, battles suffering and prosperity. 

DLCs, the first one Brushes with death is alright it is a good quest line to finish and if you are into ART it is super cool but it's nothing mind blowing. Now LEGACY OF THE FORGE, omg this is soooo good you have a forge and you are an official blacksmith with quest and upgrades to the forge and armor and customization and everything, absolutely lovely. The third one Mysteria Ecclesiae is the mission from KCD 1 where you were a monk, just in a bigger map and you are basically a detective not a monk. Absolutely lovely the setting is stunning, quest is awesome and activities also. All in all DLC are bloody awesome.

At the writing of this review I have 184 hours in the game finished it once and began a second playtrough in hardcore seeking 100% achievements. I will finish the second playtrough around 250-300 hours in. After that I can play it with my friends in multiplayer which I am excited about. Because there is new MULTIPLAYER mod made for this game. I am so thrilled. I don't know why, but I can feel the love which was put into this game by the devs and also by the community and it feels just right.

[h1] KCD2 is a masterpiece [/h1]

I have sunk an unhealthy amount of hours into the game but somehow still find myself discovering new things. Little interactions, hidden details, unexpected consequences storytelling that makes one stop and stare at a random corner of the world like one has just unearthed a lost Shakespearean tragedy. This game is so ridiculously rich in detail that I genuinely wonder how much of it I will have to play before I can confidently say I have seen everything. At this rate I will be on my deathbed finding the first time NPC unique dialogue.



The characters are phenomenal. They feel like people rather than glorified quest dispensers with their own personalities, motivations, flaws and peculiarities. The writing in the game is consistently brilliant. The story manages to be compelling without sacrificing the grounded human quality that makes this world so believable. Even the mundane interactions have a certain charm to them. Warhorse somehow made talking to people walking around the countryside and getting absolutely demolished in a fight feel like components of an unforgettable experience.



The mechanics? Magnificent. The combat has weight the progression feels earned and the sheer number of systems that interact with one another makes the world feel genuinely alive. Every action feels like it belongs in the setting and every little thing you learn makes you feel like a player manipulating game mechanics and more like an actual person learning to survive in medieval Bohemia. The immersion is borderline absurd. I don't merely play this game; I temporarily relocate to the century and develop personal grievances against people who probably died six hundred years ago.



The environmental storytelling deserves recognition too. The world is not a pretty backdrop for your next objective. It is a place with history, character and a life of its own. There are stories told through architecture, landscapes, the placement of objects and the little details you would miss entirely if you were sprinting from quest marker to quest marker like a dopamine-addicted lunatic. Kingdom Come: Deliverance II rewards curiosity in a way few games do and that is perhaps its greatest achievement.



What impresses me most is that despite the hundreds of hours I have poured into it the game still manages to surprise me. There is always something to discover some mechanic I haven't fully appreciated some detail that makes me reconsider an earlier experience. It is the sort of game that reminds you why video games can be an art form in their right.



Warhorse Studios has created something special here. Not just a great RPG, A world I genuinely love spending time in. The passion, craftsmanship and sheer ambition behind this game are extraordinary. I could spend another thousand hours in Bohemia. Still find reasons to come back for more.



If Warhorse Studios ever asks me to sacrifice my firstborn in exchange for Kingdom Come: Deliverance III I will need three seconds to consider the offer.. Those three seconds will be spent checking whether the sacrifice is a mandatory quest objective or an optional side quest.



10/10. A monumental achievement, in RPG design. Henrys come to see us. I have absolutely no intention of letting him leave.

In short: this is an amazingly detailed, large and fun game that despite some minor shortcomings you should definitely play.

The long version is that KCD2 is the successor to KCD1, which I feel people forget because of all the hype and awards KCD2 has gotten at release. If you are on the fence of playing KCD1 or not, definitely do! It introduces many of the characters you meet, is maybe a bit less polished but equally fun. While I agree you won't miss that much, a lot of details will go pass you, and the devil is in the details :)

Back to KCD2, so you continue off as Henry from KCD1. The story is much more different compared to the original. You continue your revenge story, but aside from that you are heavily mixed up in the war between Wenceslas and Sigismund. Aside from those 2, there are dozens of other characters involved that in their turn involve Henry. I honestly gave up on the story half-way through because I just couldn't follow what we were actually doing. The scope of things diminishes near the later quests and I felt the story got better their. 
The side quests are much more enjoyable and personal, while not being repetitive or fetch-quests, so go out of your way to do them, since there are a lot. I got the achievement for doing most things in the same about 40 hours from actually I did everything, so there is plenty of choice.

Graphics and music are great; the game looks really beautiful and performance is rock solid. Not much to add in that department.

Its an RPG with a plethora of skills, so you have great variety in how you want to play. Using your sword/mace/axe/hammer and bash skulls in, optionally boosting your skills with alchemy. Or being a sneaky guy picking people of with a (cross)bow and dagger. Or just talking your way out of everything. Its all possible and rarely are you forced to a single solution (minus some stealth-only segments here and there). Most other skills take a backseat and usually come in handy but don't influence the general flow of things much (like dog/horse handling, reading, crafting, survival or drinking). The one other useful - if not the most useful - is thievery. Even if you want to roleplay as someone who never steals or pickpockets, its very handy to be able to open certain doors and chests with a high enough lockpicking skill.

Medieval people like fighting, so you will have to pull out your weapon eventually. The combat is probably the most divisive element of KCD2 and most negative reviews are about this. Its not a hack and slash you have to approach combat with a bit more realism and fighting anything over 3 enemies at the same time will probably result in a death screen. There's essentially 4 directions you can attack from and parrying and countering are important skills to learn. Learn the masterstrike early to make things easier but its definitely nerfed coming from KCD1. I wouldn't call the combat bad, but I agree with people saying it's annoying at times.

The DLC's are also worth. If you were to pick one, I would say Legacy of the Forge since it has the most to offer but Brushes with Death and Mysteria Ecclesiae are equally good. I see some people hating on Mysteria but I really enjoyed it. You can play most DLC's as you encounter them - especially Legacy - but I would keep Mysteria for after the main quest.

So yeah, aside from the combat being a bit flaky at times and the story being real convoluted halfway through, everything else is just fantastic and you should play this game.

[h3]I came here to live[/h3]

A lot has changed between the time I played the first game and the second. Funnily enough, given the setting, in the meantime, I got into historical reenactment, larp and fencing. I became a bit of a handcrafter, a bit of a historian, and a bit of a swordsman

Naturally, I approached KCD2 with a much more critical eye than I did the first game. Honestly, I never even considered the KCD a masterpiece, so the sequel didn't exactly have an enormous amount of goodwill to burn through. KCD was solid, sure, but it never lived up to the “second Witcher” hype people kept throwing around at the time.

And then KCD2 somehow became that game. It completely surprised me and made me fall for it hard, even though I was looking at it with way more skepticism.


[b]Once you get invested in the story, it doesn't let go until the very end.[/b]


This is storytelling in the truest sense of the word. Not just some excuse for the protagonist to exist in an open world, as is the case with so many games, but one coherent, genuinely compelling story.

It has fantastic twists, memorable characters, moments that are both heartbreaking and hilarious, and dialogue that rarely lets you get bored. Every second or third cutscene had me going "♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, how the hell did they pull that off? These absolute madmen"

Taking this story in felt as good as it must have felt for the developers to make it. This is genuine art. It's not another game that sucks the life out of you in exchange for a hundred pointless activities. This thing was made with love, and it lets you feel as though you're living another life.


[b]And that "another life" thing applies to the characters too.[/b]


You can feel that the actors weren’t just playing these roles, they were living them I randomly stumbled across videos and streams featuring Tom McKay (Henry) and/or Luke Dale (Hans), and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, these guys seem to live and breathe this game even outside of work. Luke Dale genuinely seems to identify with the character he played, even in real life. That's an incredible level of commitment to a role.

That kind of dedication is rare, and from what I can tell it was shared by a huge part of the development team and cast. That’s what makes this world feel alive. The more you dig into the people behind the game and watch stuff about the development process, the more you realize just how much love and soul went into it.


[b]That said, it wasn’t all smooth sailing.[/b]


The game still has bugs and some unbalanced, poorly thought-out moments, although far fewer than the first one.

Combat is still far from perfect. What really pisses me off is the continued existence of "ice skating" - when your positions sync up for animations. If an opponent parries your attack from a distance, he’ll just slide toward you like he’s on ice so the animation can play out.

It completely kills any sense of weapon range. Polearms especially feel pointless; a guy with a short mace or sword will just skate right up into your face so he can ignore the reach advantage your longsword or a spear is supposed to give you. From my own time spent fencing, I’ve learned that not only the length of your sword, but even your height and the length of your arms actually matter in a fight - but none of that matters in the game.

On top of that, Henry constantly gets stuck on branches and rocks in fights, his movement becomes sluggish, and since you can’t look down at your feet during combat, it gets really annoying - especially when you’re trying to backpedal while fighting ten guys at once.

Some quests are needlessly, almost sadistically convoluted. It doesn't happen too often but sometimes you’ll get something like: "Find Zbysek. Last person who saw him was Jesek. Jesek has disappeared, so go talk to Pasek. None of them will tell you anything until you talk to ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ first. They're all in different towns, so enjoy running around the map talking to fifteen different people who have nothing more interesting to say. Congratulations, you've finally found Zbyshek." It was annoying, but truth be told, there are only a handful of quests like that.

And that’s pretty much the entire list of real complaints. For a modern AAA game, that’s a short list. It’s a price I’m more than willing to pay for the immersion this game delivers. The game is worth almost every single hour you put into it.


In the end, [b]I din't play this game. I lived here[/b]


Because even when you're not following the gripping main story or doing interesting quests, Kingdom Come: Deliverance 2 is one of the best immersive sims out there. When you boot it up, you won't be thinking "I’ll just knock out a couple of quests" or, worse, "I’ll clear a few outposts and do some dailies"

You will be thinking "I’m going in there to live"

Because ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, you really do live in this game. I don’t know how these absolute maniacs pulled it off, but sometimes it’s pure joy just walking through a medieval town, stumbling into random events, taking part in this life, competing in tournaments, walking into any house and looking at how people live, then riding out into the fields, finding a pasture full of cows and going up to each one going "hello, cow" chasing around ridiculous squealing little piglets, or just looking at the beautiful horses. The only thing missing is the ability to set up camp like in RDR2.

And a special mention goes to the blacksmithing. As someone who genuinely appreciates the craft, I spent a ridiculous amount of time in this game just forging things.

That's the magic of it. There's always something to do, but you don't always need a quest marker telling you what it is. Sometimes you just want to exist in this world for a while.

That's ultimately the best thing I can say about Kingdom Come: Deliverance 2. It's a literal window into another world. It has a gripping story and a living, breathing environment that's a joy to immerse yourself in, even when you're doing absolutely nothing of importance.

In the end, this game completely won me over. My appreciation for it is on an entirely different level. It's earned a place among my all-time favorite games. I'm genuinely happy I got to spend time in this world. And someday, I'll be back.
